evidence.evidence_paraphrase: The study varies laser wavelength and liquid medium to synthesize Ag, Au, and Ag/Au nanoparticles, then drop-casts them onto filter paper for SERS substrates.
Ag/Au alloy nanoparticle sizes are compared across laser wavelengths and water versus aqueous NaCl, without a polymer-defined bridge or controlled gap series.
SERS intensity is compared among nanoparticle-loaded filter-paper substrates made under different synthesis conditions; the comparison is not a directional gap-size experiment.

assessments.scientific_rationale: The paper contains Ag-containing nanoparticles, nanoscale morphology variation, and SERS measurements, but it studies laser-ablation wavelength and liquid-medium effects rather than a polymer-separated Ag-bridge architecture with controlled inner/outer gap variation and a directional SERS response.

evidence.evidence_paraphrase: Nanoparticles are drop-cast onto filter paper and dried at room temperature; the analyte is subsequently drop-cast onto the dried substrate.
Colloidal solutions are characterized by UV–visible absorption, while Raman/SERS measurements are separately collected from prepared substrates.
The paper reports SERS intensity variation and signal decay over 60 days for dried filter-paper substrates under different nanoparticle synthesis conditions.
Reproducibility is assessed across locations on the paper substrate, and excitation-wavelength effects are measured for analytes on the optimized dried substrate.

assessments.scientific_rationale: The paper uses colloidal Ag/Au nanoparticles and dried filter-paper SERS substrates, and reports signal variation and decay, but its protocol applies nanoparticles to filter paper, dries them, and only afterward applies the analyte. This is not a paired solution-to-dried measurement of the same analyte-mixed preparation and does not establish the frozen peak-distribution or peak-profile transformation relation.
